options.text: The evaluation time of the expression, in seconds since 1970-01-01 UTC
options.note: Right. In a range query that's each step's time, not necessarily the current wall-clock time.

options.text: The current wall-clock time in milliseconds
options.note: It's seconds, and it's the evaluation time rather than strictly "now".

options.text: The timestamp of the most recent sample
options.note: That's what timestamp(v) gives for each sample.

options.text: The server's uptime
options.note: Uptime would be time() - process_start_time_seconds.

explanation: time() returns seconds since January 1, 1970 UTC. It doesn't return the current time, but the time at which the expression is evaluated.
hint: Think about range queries evaluated at many steps.

options.text: For each up series, the timestamp of its sample in seconds since the epoch
options.note: Right. timestamp(v) returns each sample's timestamp.

options.text: The current evaluation time
options.note: That's time().

options.text: The value of up multiplied by the time
options.note: It returns the sample's timestamp, not a product.

options.text: The time the target was first discovered
options.note: It only knows the sample's own timestamp.

explanation: timestamp(v instant-vector) returns the timestamp of each of the samples of the given vector as seconds since January 1, 1970 UTC.
hint: The function name tells you which part of the sample it returns.

stem: You need to know how long ago a cache was last refreshed. What should the application export?

options.text: A gauge holding the Unix timestamp of the last refresh
options.note: Right. Then compute time() - metric in PromQL.

options.text: A gauge of seconds since the last refresh, updated every second
options.note: The docs advise against this. It needs update logic that can get stuck.

options.text: A counter that increments every second
options.note: That's a hand-rolled clock that resets on restart, and a fragile way to do it.

options.text: A log line on every refresh
options.note: Logs don't give you a queryable metric.

explanation: If you want to track the amount of time since something happened, export the Unix timestamp at which it happened, not the time since. Then use time() - my_timestamp_metric.

stem: Why do the docs prefer exporting a timestamp over a "seconds since" value? Select all that apply.

options.text: It removes the need for update logic
options.note: Right. A timestamp only changes when the event happens.

options.text: It protects you against the update logic getting stuck
options.note: Right. A stuck "seconds since" value silently freezes.

options.text: It uses less disk space because timestamps compress to zero
options.note: Disk usage isn't the reason the docs give.

options.text: Prometheus can't store values larger than 86400
options.note: There's no such limit. Values are float64.

explanation: With the timestamp exported, time() - my_timestamp_metric gives the time since the event, removing the need for update logic and protecting against that logic getting stuck.
hint: Two reasons in the docs are about update logic.

stem: Which name follows the convention for a metric holding the time the last record was processed?

options.text: data_pipeline_last_record_processed_timestamp_seconds
options.note: Right. That's the docs' own example: a _timestamp_seconds suffix in base units.

options.text: data_pipeline_last_record_processed_ms
options.note: Use base units (seconds) and the timestamp_seconds suffix.

options.text: data_pipeline_last_record_processed_total
options.note: _total is for accumulating counters, not timestamps.

options.text: data_pipeline_seconds_since_last_record
options.note: That's a "time since" metric, which the docs advise against.

explanation: The naming guide's example for a timestamp tracking the latest record processed is data_pipeline_last_record_processed_timestamp_seconds.
hint: Base unit plus a word that says what kind of value it is.

stem: Client libraries export process_start_time_seconds. Which expression gives each process's uptime in seconds?

options.text: time() - process_start_time_seconds
options.note: Right. Evaluation time minus start time.

options.text: process_start_time_seconds - time()
options.note: This gives a negative number. Subtract the start time from time().

options.text: rate(process_start_time_seconds[5m])
options.note: It's a gauge holding a timestamp, and it doesn't increase.

options.text: timestamp(process_start_time_seconds)
options.note: That's when the sample was scraped, not when the process started.

explanation: process_start_time_seconds is the start time of the process since the Unix epoch, in seconds. time() - metric gives the time elapsed since the event.

stem: What do the docs name as the key metric of a batch job?

options.text: The last time it succeeded
options.note: Right. Usually exported as a timestamp gauge and pushed to the Pushgateway.

options.text: Its total CPU seconds
options.note: That can be useful, but it isn't the key metric the docs name.

options.text: The number of log lines it wrote
options.note: Not the key metric.

options.text: Its average memory usage
options.note: Not the key metric.

explanation: The key metric of a batch job is the last time it succeeded. It's also useful to track stage durations, overall runtime and the last completion time. These are gauges, pushed to a Pushgateway.
hint: For a job that runs nightly, what do you most need to know?

stem: A gauge job_last_success_timestamp_seconds is set when a job succeeds. Which expression is true when the last success was more than 1 day ago?

options.text: time() - job_last_success_timestamp_seconds > 86400
options.note: Right. Elapsed seconds compared with one day (86,400 s).

options.text: job_last_success_timestamp_seconds > 86400
options.note: That compares an absolute timestamp with 86,400, which is always true for any recent date.

options.text: rate(job_last_success_timestamp_seconds[1d]) == 0
options.note: rate is for counters, and this gauge isn't one.

options.text: time() - job_last_success_timestamp_seconds > 1
options.note: Units are seconds, so 1 would mean one second.

explanation: time() - my_timestamp_metric gives the time since the event in seconds. Compare it with 86400 for one day.

stem: What does day_of_week() return when called with no argument?

options.text: The current evaluation time's weekday in UTC, from 0 (Sunday) to 6
options.note: Right. It defaults to vector(time()) and uses UTC.

options.text: The weekday in the server's local timezone, from 1 (Monday) to 7
options.note: It's UTC, and 0 means Sunday.

options.text: The number of days since the epoch
options.note: That isn't what it returns.

options.text: An error, because an argument is required
options.note: The argument defaults to vector(time()).

explanation: day_of_week(v=vector(time())) interprets values as Unix timestamps and returns the day of the week in UTC, from 0 to 6, where 0 means Sunday.
hint: Weeks start on Sunday here, and the timezone is always UTC.

options.text: The UTC hour (0 to 23) in which each process started
options.note: Right. The function reads the value as a Unix timestamp.

options.text: The number of hours each process has been running
options.note: That would be (time() - process_start_time_seconds) / 3600.

options.text: The current hour
options.note: With an argument, it uses the argument's values, not the current time.

options.text: The hour when the sample was scraped
options.note: It uses the sample value, which here is the start time, not the scrape timestamp.

explanation: hour(v) interprets float sample values as Unix timestamps and returns the hour of the day in UTC (0 to 23) for each.
hint: Date functions read the sample value as a timestamp.

stem: Should an exporter normally attach its own timestamps to the samples it exposes?

options.text: No. Let Prometheus assign the scrape time
options.note: Right. The exporter guide says not to set timestamps on exposed metrics.

options.text: Yes, always, for accuracy
options.note: The guide says the opposite.

options.text: Yes, but only in seconds
options.note: Exposition timestamps would be milliseconds anyway, and the guide advises against setting them.

options.text: Only for counters
options.note: The advice applies to all metrics.

explanation: Exporter scrapes should be synchronous, and you should not set timestamps on the metrics you expose. Let Prometheus take care of that.
hint: Who knows best when a scrape happened?
